blocks.value: In programming, you may want to write code usable by **more than one type with the same underlying behavior**. You do not want to repeat your code line by line, changing only which data types it can access. For example, `setValue()` and `getValue()` should be able to set and retrieve types besides `String`.
**Generic types (or generics) associate one or more non-specified Java types upon creation. They are declared within angle brackets `<>`.**

**`public class Gen<T>`**: `T` is the name of a **type parameter**, a placeholder for the actual type passed to `Gen` when an object is created. Because `Gen` uses a type parameter, it is a **generic class**, also called a **parameterized type**.

There is no special significance to the name `T`; any valid identifier would work, but `T` is traditional. **It is recommended that type parameter names be single-character capital letters.** The most commonly used are:
**`private T data;`**: `T` declares an object called `data`, which will be of the type passed to `T`. If `String` is passed, `data` is a `String` in that instance.
**`public void setValue(T dt)`**: the parameter's actual type is determined by the type passed to `T`. Because both `dt` and `data` are of type `T`, they are the same actual type for a given object.
**`public T getValue()`**: a type parameter can also specify a method's return type.

**`showType()`** displays the type of `T` by calling `getName()` on the `Class` object returned by `getClass()` on `data`. **`getClass()` is defined by `Object`**, so it is a member of all class types, and returns a `Class` object corresponding to the object's class. `Class` defines **`getName()`**, which returns a string representation of the class name.
